newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks rise, legislated settlement scorned.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks rise, legislated settlement scorned.

text.p: Shares of tobacco companies rallied across the board Monday after an Indiana jury acquitted major U.S. tobacco marketers Friday in a liability suit brought by a deceased smoker's widow, analysts said.

On the New York Stock Exchange, shares of Philip Morris Cos Inc were up 2-5/8 at 90-5/8, paring earlier gains from a session high of 92-1/8. RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, parent company of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, was up 1-1/4 at 26-5/8, while other tobacco companies were higher by 1-3/8 to 1/4.
The verdict in favor of the tobacco industry in the Rogers case eased tensions in a stock-market sector that analysts say is grossly undervalued as a result of litigation pressures.

Industry observers took a dim view of an article in Monday's Wall Street Journal that claimed legislation intended to create a broad settlement of most of the lawsuits was circulating quietly on Capitol Hill.

The article said congressional leaders were drafting a bill that would give cigarette makers protection from liability suits and prevent government regulation of tobacco in exchange for a multibillion-dollar payout to settle litigation.

Fourteen states currently are seeking reimbursement for Medicaid funds spent on smoking-related illnesses, most in suits that seek a billion dollars or more. Hundreds of personal-injury suits and class-action lawsuits also hang over the industry.
"It's a good concept, but I'm not sure there is the political sentiment for it yet," said Salomon Brothers analyst Diana Temple.
RJR Nabisco responded to the article by saying it "has not had any negotiations with anyone...concerning this subject" and that the specifics of the article were "completely unrealistic."
Analysts said that it was more than likely that discussion of some kind concerning an industrywide settlement had occurred in the backrooms of major tobacco companies.
"I think that they're discussing it. They almost have to," said Ronald Morrow, an analyst at Rodman & Renshaw.
But legislation is unlikely to emerge from those backrooms because both sides of the skirmish feel they have the other on the run, Morrow said.
Although plaintiffs lost in Indiana, an August 9 victory in Florida -- where a former smoker was awarded $750,000 in damages -- may have their attorneys feeling new-found strength.
"As long as the plaintiffs feel they're in Fat City, don't look for any sort of meaningful compromise," said Emanuel Goldman, an analyst at PaineWebber.
"For the first time, they won a case. You think they're suddenly going to become accommodative? This is not the kind of environment where you get an agreement," Goldman said.

Morrow said Philip Morris shares could return to the high 90s this week, largely on expectations that a directors' meeting on Wednesday will yield a dividend increase of 18 percent to 20 percent and a stock split.
